blocks.text: [II, 739] ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE [col. 161] PART TWO BOOK TWO ON ON THE UNCLEAN BIRDS.
CHAPTER I.
The eagle, king of the birds; its name, beak, talons, plumage, baldness, renewal, colour.

In this book we shall set out the unclean birds in the same order as Moses in Levit. XI, 13. and Deut. XIV, 2. First of all is the eagle. To this pertains what Baal Hatturim has here: פתח בנשר שהוא מלך בעופות, He began with the eagle, because it is king of the birds. That is, in the list of those birds whose eating God forbade the Jews, he holds that the eagle rightly leads the line, since the consensus of nations has given it kingship over the other birds because of the outstanding gifts by which it surpasses them. As to the Greeks the matter is plain. For Pindar, Olymp. 13, calls the eagle
— — οἰωνῶν βασιλῆα [oiōnōn basilēa],
king of the birds. And Pyth. 1:
Διὸς αἰετὸν, ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν [Dios aieton, archon oiōnōn],
the eagle of Jupiter, leader of the birds. And Isthm. 6:
— — — ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν μέγαν αἰετὸν [archon oiōnōn megan aieton],
the prince of the birds, the great eagle. And the oracle about the Athenians in the Knights [col. 162] of Aristophanes, Act 3:
Αἰετὸς ὡς γίνει, καὶ πάσης γῆς βασιλεύσεις [Aietos hōs ginei, kai pasēs gēs basileuseis],
Be like an eagle, and you will rule the whole world. Nicander too, where he speaks of the fight of the eagle and the serpent, Theriaca, line 448:
[II, 740] Τῷ μέν τ᾽ ἔκπαγλον κοτέων βασιλήϊος ὄρνις Αἰετὸς, — — — — — — [Tō men t᾽ ekpaglon koteōn basilēios ornis Aietos]

But against him the royal bird, the eagle, raging in monstrous fashion. And Boeus, in book 1 of the Ornithogonia, on Periphas, changed by Jupiter into an eagle: Ποιεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὄρνισι βασιλέα [Poiei gar auton en pasi tois ornisi basilea]. For he makes him king among all the birds. And Dionysius in the Bassarica, cited by Stephanus under Κάσπειρος [Kaspeiros]:
Αἰετὸς εἰν ὄρνισι μεταπρέπει ἀγρομένοισιν [Aietos ein ornisi metaprepei agromenoisin],
The eagle excels among the wild birds. And Quintus Smyrnaeus, book 3, line 353:
Αἰετὸς οἰωνῶν προφερέστατος [Aietos oiōnōn propherestatos],
The eagle, most excellent of birds. And Oppian, Halieutica, book 2, line 539:
Ὅσσον γὰρ κέφοισι μετ᾽ οἰωνοῖσιν ἄνακτες Αἰετοί. — — — — — — [Hosson gar kephoisi met᾽ oiōnoisin anaktes Aietoi]

As much as among the light birds the eagles, their kings (excel). And Aelian, Hist. book 9, ch. [col. 163] 2: Τὸν ἀετὸν, τὸν τῶν ὀρνίθων βασιλέα, οὐ μόνον παρόντα, καὶ ζῶντα δέδοικε τὰ ὄρνεα [Ton aeton, ton tōn ornithōn basilea, ou monon paronta, kai zōnta dedoike ta ornea]; The birds fear the eagle, king of the birds, not only when it is alive and present. Finally Philes calls it πτηνοκράτορα [ptēnokratora], that is, prince of the birds. And Tzetzes, Chiliad. 5, Hist. 9, denies that either eagles or lions touch carrion, since they are kings, the former of birds, the latter of wild beasts. And among the Roman writers, Horace, book 4, Ode 4:
Like the winged minister of the thunderbolt, to whom the king of the gods granted kingship over the wandering birds, etc.
Martial, book 5, Epigram 56:
Tell me whom you carry, queen of the birds.
Apuleius, The Ass, book 6: that royal bird of supreme Jupiter. Claudian, Preface to the Third Consulship of Honorius:
— — both mighty over the birds and heir of the thunderbolt.
